title: Fast-forward and three-way merges
summary: git merge either slides a pointer forward or creates a merge commit from the merge base. Know which one you will get before you run it.

steps.title: Fast-forward
body: You are on `main` and run `git merge feature`. If `main`'s tip is an **ancestor** of `feature`, nothing has happened on `main` since feature branched off. Git just slides the pointer:
No new commit, no conflicts possible. History stays a straight line.
`git merge --no-ff feature` forces a merge commit anyway, which some teams like so that every feature shows up as one merge in `main`'s history.

steps.prompt: `main` is at B and `feature` is `B---C---D`. You run `git switch main` then `git merge feature`. What does `git log --oneline` print? Use the letters as hashes and the messages `Add C`, `Add D`, and so on.
code: # A: "Add A", B: "Add B", C: "Add C", D: "Add D"
steps.explain: A fast-forward: `main` now points at D, so its log is the feature commits on top of the old main. No merge commit was created.

steps.title: Three-way merge
body: If both branches have new commits, a pointer slide is impossible. Git does a **three-way merge** using three snapshots:
1. Find the **merge base**: the best common ancestor (B).
2. Compare base->ours and base->theirs file by file, line by line.
3. A change made on only one side is taken. The same change on both sides is taken once. **Different** changes to the same lines are a **conflict**.
4. Record merge commit M with **two parents**: E (first parent, the branch you were on) and F.

steps.prompt: Why does Git need the merge base, rather than just comparing `main` with `feature`?
options: Without the base it cannot tell which side changed a line: two differing versions alone do not say who edited and who kept the original
To find the author of each line
Because comparing two tips is too slow
It only needs it for fast-forwards
steps.explain: If main says `x = 1` and feature says `x = 2`, the base tells you who changed it. Base `x = 1` means only feature changed it, so take feature's line. No conflict.

steps.prompt: For each line, what does a three-way merge produce? Write the result line, or `CONFLICT`. Base, ours and theirs are given per line.
steps.explain: Line 1: only theirs changed. Line 2: only ours changed. Line 3: both made the same change. Line 4: both changed it differently, so Git cannot choose.

steps.prompt: Will `git merge feature` (run on `main`) fast-forward or create a merge commit?
steps.explain: Fast-forward is only possible when the branch you are on has nothing new of its own.

steps.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: the best common ancestor of the two tips
moving the pointer along; no new commit
the branch you were on when you merged

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: show the merge base of `main` and `feature`, then merge `feature` always creating a merge commit.
steps.explain: `git merge --ff-only` is the opposite safety switch: it refuses unless a fast-forward is possible. `--squash` stages the combined changes without making a merge commit.

steps.title: Find the merge base
prompt: 1. Collect every ancestor of `a` (including `a`) into a set.
2. Walk from `b` **breadth-first** (a queue), visiting parents in the order listed. Return the first commit you meet that is in the set.
3. Return `null` if there is none (unrelated histories).
D <- E            MergeBase("B", "E") = "B"   (B is already an ancestor: fast-forward)
starter: static string? MergeBase(string a, string b, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents)
solution: static HashSet<string> Ancestors(string start, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents)

Then BFS from `b` with a `Queue<string>`; check membership before enqueueing parents.
Keep a visited set for the BFS too, so merges do not loop.
